name: Anthropomorphism
description: People attribute human traits, feelings, intentions, or motives to non-human things such as products, bots, brands, animals, or algorithms. Human-like cues invite social interpretation.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to conversational AI, chatbots, assistants, mascots, and interface tone: names, avatars, first-person language, typing indicators, apologies, and turn-taking cues can make users over-attribute understanding, empathy, agency, or accountability to the system.
prevalence_note: A standard concept in chatbot, robotics, voice-interface, avatar, and AI-assistant design discussions, though less universally foundational across all design work than classic judgment-and-decision biases.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of 108 independent samples (N=11,053) found anthropomorphism's effect on customers' intention to use service robots/chatbots/AI is real but genuinely moderated -- by customer traits (e.g. computer anxiety), sociodemographics (gender), robot design features, robot characteristics (intelligence), and service type (possession-processing vs. mental stimulus-processing). Functional characteristics (usefulness) mediate the effect more strongly than relational characteristics (rapport). Directly clarifies when anthropomorphic design cues help vs. hurt use intention in AI/chatbot/robot interfaces.
findings.source_title: Understanding anthropomorphism in service provision: a meta-analysis of physical robots, chatbots, and other AI
findings.source_venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

findings.description: Anthropomorphism is the attribution of humanlike characteristics, motivations, intentions, or emotions to nonhuman agents, and the reviewed literature supports a three-factor account in which anthropomorphism becomes more likely when human knowledge is salient, effectance motivation is high, and social connection is lacking.
findings.source_title: On seeing human: A three-factor theory of anthropomorphism.

applications.title: ChatGPT users attributing human-like qualities during a qualitative usability study
applications.description: NN/g conducted a qualitative usability study with professionals and students using ChatGPT in their day-to-day work, using it as the primary case study to demonstrate varying degrees of anthropomorphism -- from casual personification in language to users forming stronger perceived-relationship attributions toward the AI.
applications.ethical_note: Whether an AI system encouraging some degree of anthropomorphic perception is user-beneficial (more approachable, easier to interact with naturally) or a risk (emotional over-reliance on a non-human system) is a genuinely live, unresolved question in this space, not something this specific source resolves either way -- graded unclear rather than assigning a confident verdict, distinct from cases in this corpus with no ethical dimension at all (not_applicable) or a clearly resolved one.

applications.title: Replika users citing companionship as their primary reason for attachment to an AI
applications.description: Observations from the Replika subreddit found that users consistently cited companionship-related themes as their primary reasons for valuing their AI companion app, illustrating a stronger degree of anthropomorphism than casual personification -- users relating to the AI as something closer to a relationship than a tool.
applications.industry_context: AI companionship / mental health & wellness apps
applications.ethical_note: Unlike ChatGPT (a general-purpose tool where anthropomorphism is a side effect of natural-language interaction), Replika is explicitly designed as a companionship product -- deliberately engineered for emotional attachment. That's a real, structural difference worth naming: the ethical stakes of anthropomorphism scale with how deliberately a product cultivates the perception of relationship, not just whether the perception occurs at all.
